course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best summarizes Mill's argument in the passage?
choices: Liberty applies only to societies he considered advanced

stimulusBlocks.attribution: John Stuart Mill, British philosopher and official of the East India Company from 1823 to 1858, On Liberty, 1859
stimulusBlocks.citation: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, ch. 1, Introductory. Project Gutenberg eBook #34901.
stimulusBlocks.note: “This doctrine” is Mill's principle that people should be free to act as they choose unless they harm others. “Nonage” means childhood or immaturity. Akbar was the Mughal emperor.
stimulusBlocks.text: It is, perhaps, hardly necessary to say that this doctrine is meant to apply only to human beings in the maturity of their faculties. . . . For the same reason, we may leave out of consideration those backward states of society in which the race itself may be considered as in its nonage. . . . Despotism is a legitimate mode of government in dealing with barbarians, provided the end be their improvement, and the means justified by actually effecting that end. Liberty, as a principle, has no application to any state of things anterior to the time when mankind have become capable of being improved by free and equal discussion. Until then, there is nothing for them but implicit obedience to an Akbar or a Charlemagne, if they are so fortunate as to find one.

Mill worked for the company that ruled India, which shaped his acceptance of rule over “backward” societies.
questions.distinguisher: Mill defended British rule in India; he did not oppose all empire.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 6.1 key concept: Europeans and Americans justified imperialism with ideologies such as Social Darwinism, nationalism, and the concept of a civilizing mission
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing Social Darwinism, c. 1860–1914
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1859 Charles Darwin argued that species change through natural selection. Writers such as Herbert Spencer, who coined the phrase “survival of the fittest,” applied similar ideas to human societies. They claimed that nations and races competed for survival and that the strongest deserved to dominate.

Scientists today reject this reasoning. Darwin's theory described biological change in species, not a ranking of human groups. But in the late 1800s, Social Darwinism gave politicians and writers a scientific-sounding justification for conquest and for racial hierarchy at home and abroad.

questions.explanation: The author says Darwin's theory described species, not a ranking of humans.
choiceExplanations: The author says scientists reject it.
Writers such as Spencer applied it.
The author rejects such ranking.
The author says Darwin's theory described species, not a ranking of humans.
questions.distinguisher: Spencer, not Darwin, applied the ideas to societies.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 6.1 key concept: a desire to spread Christianity and the concept of a civilizing mission were used to justify imperialism
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the idea of a civilizing mission, c. 1850–1914
stimulusBlocks.text:
Many Europeans believed they had a duty to bring Christianity, Western education, and their own laws to colonized peoples. Missionaries founded schools and hospitals across Africa and Asia. In 1899 the British poet Rudyard Kipling published “The White Man's Burden,” urging the United States to take up the duty of ruling the Philippines.

Colonized people often saw things differently. Mission schools could open new opportunities, and some graduates became leaders of later independence movements. But the civilizing mission assumed that colonized cultures were inferior, and it was used to justify taking land, labor, and political power.

questions.prompt: The second paragraph best supports which claim?

Mission schools had only harmful effects for everyone

questions.explanation: Schools opened opportunities while the idea assumed inferiority.
choiceExplanations: Schools had effects.
Many saw things differently.
Some graduates benefited.
Schools opened opportunities while the idea assumed inferiority.
questions.distinguisher: The passage notes that some graduates became leaders, so effects were not only harmful.
